title: Simple cable scarf
subtitle: A single travelling six-stitch cable on a reverse-stocking-stitch ground.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in a single centred six-stitch cable on a reverse-stocking-stitch ground, on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn. The cable cross happens every six rows and pulls the fabric into a pleasing raised rope that runs the full 180 cm length. Finished dimensions are 20 cm wide by 180 cm long.
sourceNotes: Simple cable scarves and comforters appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, where a central rope cable on a purl ground is described as a standard accessory pattern. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the six-stitch rope cable, citations only.
heroPrompt: A finished simple cable scarf in heathered grey aran-weight wool, laid flat on a wooden surface showing the raised rope cable running down the centre against the purl ground, natural daylight.

glossaryTerms.definition: Place 3 stitches on a cable needle and hold at the front of the work, knit the next 3 stitches from the left needle, then knit the 3 stitches from the cable needle. This crosses the cable to the left and produces a rope that twists towards the viewer.
Stocking stitch with the purl face used as the right side. On a flat piece, knit across on wrong-side rows and purl across on right-side rows, so the purl bumps face outward.
A cast-on that forms a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

Holding a steam iron a few centimetres above the finished piece and allowing steam to penetrate the fabric, then smoothing to shape and leaving to dry. Used for cables: wetting cables can kill their raised definition.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat from one short end to the other, centring a single six-stitch rope cable on a reverse-stocking-stitch ground, finishing at 20 cm wide and 180 cm long. The cable cross happens every six rows using a cable needle and pulls three stitches past three others to produce a raised left-twist rope. The reverse-stocking-stitch ground makes the cable stand out clearly with no other pattern to compete with it.

Flat construction was chosen because a cabled scarf worked flat has two straight edges that lie flat without seaming and a fabric that the cable holds stable without curling. The finished scarf needs about 350 m (approximately 200 g) of aran-weight yarn. The cable slightly narrows the fabric, so the piece pulls in to about 20 cm from a cast-on of 36 stitches that would give 22 cm in plain stocking stitch. The scarf is warm and substantial and wraps once around the neck with both ends hanging to the chest.

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Wool gives the best stitch definition for cables. Acrylic can be used but the cable relief will be less crisp.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer

items.name: Cable needle
items.qty: 1 (or a double-pointed needle of similar size)
items.substitutions: A short double-pointed needle in the same or similar size works in place of a cable needle.

content.text: 18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. In cable and reverse stocking stitch the gauge pulls in to approximately 16 sts per 10 cm because cables consume extra yarn to travel across each other. Swatch a 20-stitch panel including the cable cross, measure across the centre without stretching. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.25 cm at this stitch count: 17 sts per 10 cm gives about 21 cm width; 15 sts per 10 cm gives about 24 cm. Row gauge drift across the full 396 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
K (knit): insert right needle from left to right through the front of the stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl): insert right needle from right to left through the front of the stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn, draw loop through to the back.
: slip 3 stitches to a cable needle and hold at the front of the work. Knit the next 3 stitches from the left needle. Then knit the 3 stitches from the cable needle. The cable crosses to the left.
is stocking stitch with the purl face as the right side. Purl across on RS rows (outside the cable stitches) and knit across on WS rows.

to place 36 stitches on the needle. The stitch layout from right to left on right-side rows is: P15 (reverse stocking stitch), K6 (cable panel), P15 (reverse stocking stitch). Before beginning, calculate the tail length: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 36 stitches: (15.7 x 36) / 10 + 15 = 56.5 + 15 = about 72 cm. Leave a tail of at least 72 cm before the slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Row 1 (RS, cable row): P15, C6F, P15. (36 sts)
Repeat rows 1 to 6 until the scarf measures 180 cm from the cast-on edge measured along the straight grain. At the halfway mark (approximately row 198, around 90 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 198 you should have 36 stitches on the needle.

Work a standard bind-off on a right-side row: work each stitch in pattern (purl the purl stitches, knit the cable stitches) and pass the previous stitch over each new one in turn. A cable bind-off on a reverse-stocking-stitch ground can pucker if worked too tightly: aim for a loose, relaxed tension throughout.

Cable crossing in the wrong direction. C6F crosses to the left. If your rope twists to the right, you are holding the cable needle at the back rather than the front. Place the cable needle at the front of the work, between you and the main needle, before knitting the three left-needle stitches.

Dropped cable-needle stitches during the cross. Slip the three stitches to the cable needle purlwise to avoid twisting them, and keep the cable needle close to the main needle while knitting the next three stitches. A straight double-pointed needle is less likely to drop than a curved cable needle for some knitters.

Stitch count rising after a cable row. If you knit or purl an extra stitch during the cable cross, the count rises by one. Count the cable stitches before and after the cross: six stitches go onto the cable needle, six come off after the cross.
Weave in both tails along the purl-ground edge, changing direction once to secure.

is recommended for cables. Hold a steam iron 2 to 3 cm above the surface and allow steam to penetrate without pressing down onto the cables; pressing flattens the raised definition. Pat the purl ground gently to even it out and leave flat to dry. Do not wet-block cables unless the yarn label recommends it; wetting can relax the cable structure.

Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Support the full wet weight of the scarf. Press out water gently, roll in a towel, and lay flat to dry without stretching the cables lengthwise. Do not tumble dry wool cables.

Once the six-stitch cross feels comfortable, try the four-stitch cable scarf for a tighter, faster rope, or the cable-and-rib scarf which combines a cable panel with a flanking rib. The mock cable scarf is a useful detour if you want a similar raised look without a cable needle.
